# Harbourlight Analytics Employee Handbook

## 1. Welcome and Our Values

Welcome to Harbourlight Analytics. If you are reading this, you have successfully navigated the interview process and made the exciting decision to join us. We are a small, growing team of data consultants, and while we have expanded from eight to thirty people in just eighteen months, we are careful not to let size change the way we treat each other. We are a team of colleagues, not a family, but we are a team that trusts its people to do good work, to be honest with one another, and to take care of themselves and their careers.

This handbook is written for you. It is not a legal contract designed to restrict your freedom, nor is it a rulebook created by lawyers who have never done the work you do. It is a guide. It explains how things work here, what you can expect from us, and what we expect from you. We believe that when expectations are clear, anxiety goes down and creativity goes up. If you know the rules of the road, you can focus on driving the car, not worrying about whether you are allowed to drive.

We have tried to keep this document practical. If a rule has a number attached to it, the number is exact. If a process has steps, we have listed them. If something is open to interpretation, we have said so. You should read this through in your first week. Keep it handy. When a question arises about pay, leave, or equipment, this is the first place to look. It replaces the scattered documents and the tribal knowledge currently held in a few people’s heads, so please rely on this as the single source of truth for our policies.

But before we get into the mechanics of working here, we want to talk about the heart of the company: our values. At Harbourlight, we don’t use values as decorative posters on the wall. We use them as decision-making tools. When you are unsure about how to handle a difficult client request, or how to give feedback to a colleague, or how to structure a project, ask yourself which of these four values applies. These four principles—Be candid, Own the outcome, Make it simple, and Leave room for others—are the lens through which we evaluate success, hire new colleagues, and resolve conflicts.

### Be candid

Candour is the lifeblood of trust. It means being direct, honest, and transparent, even when the truth is uncomfortable. It does not mean being rude, blunt, or aggressive; it means respecting your colleague enough to tell them what you really think, rather than letting them fail because you wanted to be polite. In a consultancy, silence is often more expensive than a difficult conversation. If you see a risk, you speak up. If you disagree with a strategy, you say so. If you are struggling, you admit it.

**In practice:** Imagine you are reviewing a junior analyst’s code and you see a methodological error that will skew their results. You could wait for the final report to come out and correct it then, saving them the immediate embarrassment. Or, you could be candid. You send them a message saying, "I noticed this error in your data cleaning step. Here is why it’s wrong, and here is how to fix it. Let’s chat for ten minutes so you don’t make the same mistake on the next project." You save them time, you improve the quality of the work, and you help them learn. That is candour.

Another example: If you are overwhelmed and cannot meet a deadline, do not go silent. Do not hope the client won’t notice until the last minute. Be candid with your manager and your team as soon as you know. Say, "I underestimated the complexity of this query. I am at 50% capacity and will miss the Tuesday deadline. Here is what I can deliver by Thursday." This allows the team to adjust resources without panic and maintains the client’s trust in our transparency.

### Own the outcome

At a consultancy, you are not just a pair of hands typing code or a voice on a call. You are a partner in the result. "Own the outcome" means you care about the final result as much as your manager does. It means you look beyond the immediate task to see what the client actually needs. It means if something breaks, you don’t just report the breakage; you propose a fix. It means you do not say "that’s not my job" if you see a gap that could be filled.

**In practice:** You are sent to a client site to pull a specific dataset. You realize the data is messy and the specific pull they asked for is technically possible but useless for their business question. A passive approach is to pull the messy data, send it, and say, "Here is what you asked for." Owning the outcome means you pause. You call the stakeholder, explain why the requested data is flawed, and propose a cleaner, more relevant dataset that answers their actual business question. You take responsibility for the value we deliver, not just the hours we bill.

Another example: If a tool breaks during a live presentation, you don’t blame IT or the vendor in front of the client. You own the moment. You troubleshoot calmly, have a backup plan ready, and afterwards, you document the issue so it doesn’t happen again. You ensure the client leaves the meeting with the confidence that we handled the situation professionally, regardless of whose fault the technical glitch was.

### Make it simple

Data complexity is our job, but complexity for its own sake is our enemy. "Make it simple" means we strive for clarity in our communication, our code, and our processes. We respect our colleagues’ and clients’ time by stripping away the unnecessary. In a world of big data, simplicity is a competitive advantage. It means we value elegance over cleverness.

**In practice:** When writing a report or an email, ask yourself: Can I say this in half the words? Can I explain this chart to someone who has never used our software? If your code has three nested loops where one clean function would do, refactor it. If your presentation has twenty slides when ten would convey the message, cut it down. Simplicity is harder than complexity because it requires thinking deeply, but it is always more valuable.

Another example: When onboarding a new hire, don’t send them a link to a folder with 40 disorganized PDFs. Create a simple, curated checklist. Make it simple for others to help you. Make it simple for others to understand you. If you find yourself explaining a process for the third time in a week, it is likely the process is too complex. Simplify it.

### Leave room for others

We are small. We interact constantly. "Leave room for others" is about empathy and collaboration. It means recognizing that your way is not the only way. It means listening before you speak. It means understanding that your colleague might be struggling with a personal issue, or a health issue, or a technical blocker, and giving them the space to handle it with dignity. It is about creating an environment where everyone feels safe to contribute.

**In practice:** You are leading a brainstorming session. You have a great idea. But instead of pitching it immediately and dominating the airtime, you ask, "What do others think? Has anyone looked at this from a different angle?" You wait. You let the quieter people speak. You validate ideas that are not yours. You leave space in the conversation for the introvert in the room to find their footing.

Another example: You are working from home. Your colleague is in the office. You schedule a meeting. You don’t demand they come home to you, nor do you assume they want to come to the office. You ask what works for them. You adjust your camera and microphone to be polite on video calls. You respect their boundaries and their time zones, even if we all work in the same city. You leave room for their needs to exist alongside your own.

These values are not just words. They are the standard by which we judge success. Performance reviews, promotions, and daily feedback will often refer back to these four principles. If you are technically brilliant but dismissive of others, you are not living our values. If you are kind but let projects fail because you didn’t own the outcome, you are not living our values. We ask you to bring all four to work every day.

Who to ask: People Operations

## 2. How We Work

Now that you understand who we are, let’s look at how we operate. We are a hybrid company. Some of you are in the office every day; some are working from home most of the week; some mix and match. We do not treat you differently based on your physical location. The rules below apply to everyone, regardless of where you are sitting when you log on. Our goal is to give you the autonomy to do your best work while ensuring we remain a cohesive team.

### Working Hours and Core Time

We trust you to manage your own time. We are results-oriented, not clock-watching-oriented. However, we are a team, and we need some overlap to collaborate effectively.

Our standard working week is **37.5 hours**. You are expected to work these hours, but you have significant freedom in when you do them. We do not track your hours with timesheets, but we do expect you to be present for the work we have committed to.

To ensure we can collaborate, we have established **Core Hours**. Core hours are **10:00 to 16:00, Monday to Friday**. During these six hours, you must be available and working. This is when meetings happen, when we expect quick responses on chat, and when we expect you to be actively contributing.

Outside of core hours, you can arrange your day as you see fit. If you are an early bird, you might start at 07:00 and finish at 14:00, taking a longer break during core hours if necessary (provided your team agrees). If you are a night owl, you might start at 12:00 and work late. The key is that during 10:00–16:00, you are present and responsive.

Please communicate your working pattern to your team so they know when to expect you. This is especially important for home-based workers, so your colleagues know you are not ignoring them when you step away for lunch at 13:00. Visibility is key in a hybrid model.

### Meetings and Stand-ups

We meet to make decisions, not to perform busyness. We try to keep meetings short and purposeful. Every meeting should have a clear objective and an agenda. If you do not know why you are in a meeting, you should feel comfortable asking the organizer or leaving.

Our main daily ritual is the **Team Stand-up**. This happens every day at **10:15**. It is strictly time-boxed to 15 minutes. The format is simple: What did I do yesterday? What am I doing today? What is blocking me?

If you are leading the stand-up, keep it tight. If you are a participant, prepare your answer in advance. Do not use stand-up to solve problems; use it to flag them so people can meet afterwards to solve them. Stand-ups are for synchronization, not problem-solving.

We encourage you to decline meetings that do not have an agenda. If you are invited to a meeting and you are not required for the decision-making, ask the organizer if you can read the minutes instead. Respect your colleagues’ time by ending meetings five minutes early if you are done. This gives everyone a breather before their next commitment.

### Communication Tools

We use a limited set of tools to avoid notification fatigue. We want to keep our digital workspace clean and efficient.

1.  **Chat Tool:** We use one primary chat platform (Slack or similar, as designated by IT). This is for quick questions, collaboration, and non-urgent updates. Use it liberally for social interaction, too. This is where we share memes, celebrate wins, and ask "quick questions."
2.  **Shared Calendar:** We use one shared calendar system (Outlook or Google Calendar). Your calendar is visible to your team. Please block time for "Deep Work" if you need uninterrupted focus. This is encouraged, not frowned upon. We respect deep work time as much as meeting time.
3.  **Email:** Email is for formal communication, client-facing correspondence, and things that need a written record. It is not for urgent requests.
4.  **Phone:** Urgent requests go by **phone**, not chat. If something is critical and needs immediate attention, call. If someone does not answer, text them. Do not spam chat with "Urgent!!!" messages.

**The Rule of Urgency:** If it is urgent, call. If it is important but not urgent, email or chat. If it is complex, schedule a meeting. This hierarchy helps us manage our attention spans and ensures that genuine emergencies get immediate eyes.

### Office and Home Equity

We have one office in a mid-sized city. We have a handful of people who work mostly from home.

We treat office and home workers the same. There is no "proximity bias" at Harbourlight. Your contributions are judged by their output and impact, not by how many hours you sit at your desk.

*   **In the office:** The office is a quiet zone by default, except for the meeting pods and the kitchen. If you need to take a loud call, use a meeting pod. Keep shared spaces clean. If you finish a dish, wash it. If you finish a coffee pot, start a new one. Small courtesies go a long way in a shared space.
*   **At home:** You are responsible for your environment. Ensure you have a quiet space for meetings. Use your headset. Ensure your background is professional or blurred. You do not need to be in "business formal" attire at home, but you should be ready for video calls with clients if the situation requires it.

When we hold hybrid meetings, we follow strict etiquette to ensure equity.
1.  **Camera On (by default):** Everyone in the office and everyone at home turns their camera on. Seeing faces builds trust and helps us read non-verbal cues. If you are having a bad hair day, that’s okay—blurring is available. But generally, we want to see each other.
2.  **One Microphone Rule:** If you are in the office, only one person should use the room microphone at a time to avoid feedback loops. Home workers should mute themselves when not speaking to eliminate background noise.
3.  **Digital First:** If there is a mix of remote and in-person people, the "digital" person gets priority for the floor. The person in the office should not dominate the conversation. The facilitator should actively ask for input from the remote participants: "Sarah, you’re on mute, but do you have thoughts on this?"
4.  **Shared Screens:** All documents used in the meeting must be shared digitally via the screen share, even for those in the room, so everyone sees the same thing. Do not hold up a piece of paper to a webcam.

### Async Work

Because we do not all have identical hours, we practice asynchronous communication. This means you do not need to respond to a chat message instantly unless it is marked "Urgent."

If you are working outside core hours, do not expect an immediate reply. If you are in core hours, aim to reply to chat within 60 minutes and email within 24 hours. If you are on leave, your status is set, and you are not expected to check messages. We respect your time off.

Who to ask: Your manager

## 3. Remote and Hybrid Work

We are a hybrid company. This means we believe that work can happen anywhere, but connection happens somewhere specific. We do not believe in a rigid "all in the office" or "all remote" model. We believe in flexibility combined with intentionality. The following policy outlines how we balance autonomy with collaboration.

### Anchor Days

We recognize that physical presence matters for certain types of work—specifically, team bonding, complex brainstorming, and onboarding new hires. To ensure we get this face-to-face time without demanding it every day, we have established **Anchor Days**.

**Tuesday and Thursday** are Anchor Days. On these two days, everyone who lives within a reasonable commuting distance of the office is expected to come in. These are the days when we encourage in-person collaboration, lunch, and informal chats. If you live far away or your commute is excessive, please speak to your manager; we may be able to agree on an alternative pattern if the commute is disproportionately burdensome, but the default expectation for local staff is presence on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

The other three days of the week (Monday, Wednesday, and Friday) are flexible. On these days, you can work from wherever you work best. If you are an introvert who needs silence, work from home. If you have childcare constraints, work from home. If you need to be near a client site, work from home or the client office. The choice is yours, provided you are online during core hours.

### Fully Remote Employees

Some roles, or some individuals hired specifically for this model, are designated as **fully remote**. These employees are **exempt from Anchor Days**. You do not need to come to the office on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

However, we still believe in the power of physical connection. Fully remote employees are expected to come to the office for a **team week once per quarter**. This is a week where the whole team gathers for workshops, strategy sessions, and social time. Harbourlight Analytics covers all travel and accommodation costs for these quarterly visits. Please plan your personal schedules around these known dates, which will be published well in advance. Outside of these quarterly weeks, you work from your home office or chosen location, adhering to the same core hours and performance standards as everyone else.

### Working from Abroad

We trust you to manage your life. If you wish to work from another country—for example, to visit family or to experience a new culture—you may do so for up to **4 weeks per calendar year**.

This is **not automatic**. You must obtain **your manager's approval** first. More importantly, you must notify **People Operations at least 2 weeks before you go**. People Operations will check with local tax and employment law experts. Why? Because employment law is tied to physical location. Working from France for a month might trigger French payroll taxes or visa requirements that we cannot manage without preparation.

**Longer stays are not possible.** Due to the complexity of tax residency, social security contributions, and employment law, we cannot support employees working from abroad for longer than 4 weeks in a calendar year. This is a hard limit. If you wish to relocate internationally, this must be discussed as a formal change to your employment terms, potentially involving a new contract under local law.

### Home Office Costs

We know that working from home has costs. In addition to the one-off **€500 home-office allowance** mentioned in the Pay and Benefits chapter, we provide a **monthly internet allowance of €30**.

This allowance is paid through payroll as part of your salary package or as a reimbursement, depending on the payroll configuration. It is intended to cover the increased usage of broadband required for high-quality video conferencing and data transfer. You do not need to submit monthly receipts for this €30 allowance; it is a flat monthly benefit for all employees whose primary work location is not the company office.

### Working from Public Places

You may work from a café, library, or other public place. However, you must exercise extreme caution.

1.  **Non-Confidential Work Only:** You may **only** work on non-confidential tasks in public. Do not open client databases, do not read emails containing personal data, and do not review sensitive code snippets in a public space. A shoulder-surfing glance can cost the company a contract.
2.  **Privacy Screen Required:** You must use a **privacy screen** on your laptop. This ensures that passersby cannot read your screen.
3.  **No Overhearable Client Calls:** You must **not** take client calls in public places where you can be overheard. It is unprofessional to have a confidential business discussion in a noisy café. If you need to take a call, go to a quiet private space or return home.

### Illness

Please remember: **Working from home is not a substitute for sick leave.**

If you are too unwell to work, you must take **sick leave**. Do not try to "work from bed" because you feel guilty about taking time off. This is counterproductive; it prolongs your illness, lowers the quality of your work, and signals to the team that presenteeism is valued. If you are sick, rest. If you are well enough to work, work. But do not confuse the two. If you call in sick, you are off. You should not be checking emails or attending stand-ups.

Who to ask: Your manager

## 4. Employment Basics

This chapter covers the administrative and contractual aspects of your employment. These are the hard rules that govern your relationship with Harbourlight Analytics. While we try to keep things human, these are the legal frameworks that protect both you and the company.

### Probation Period

Every new employee starts with a **3-month probation period**. This is not a "trial" in the sense that we don’t know if you can do the job; we hired you because we believe you can. This period is about integration. It is for you to learn our systems, our clients, and our culture, and for us to support you in that transition. It is also for you to decide if Harbourlight is the right place for you.

We will not leave you to figure it out alone. We will hold a structured check-in at the end of **each month** of your probation. These are not formal performance evaluations, but they are critical milestones.

*   **Month 1 Check-in:** Focus on onboarding. Do you have the tools? Do you understand the team structure? Are you feeling supported? Are you meeting people?
*   **Month 2 Check-in:** Focus on performance. Are you meeting the initial goals? Is the workload appropriate? Are there any gaps in your training?
*   **Month 3 Check-in:** Final review. We confirm your permanent status. If there are any concerns, they will have been raised earlier. We do not surprise people at the end of probation. If things are not working out, we will know by month 2, not month 3.

During probation, notice periods are shorter to allow for flexibility. If you wish to leave, or if we need to terminate your employment, the notice period is **1 week** on either side.

After you pass probation, you become a permanent employee. The notice period increases to **4 weeks** on either side. This means if you resign, you must work four weeks (or have them paid out, at our discretion), and if we let you go, we must give you four weeks’ notice. This stability allows us to plan project resources and protects your income if the unexpected happens.

### Contract Type

Unless your offer letter explicitly states that you are on a **fixed-term** contract, your contract is permanent. Fixed-term contracts are rare and usually linked to specific project funding or maternity cover. If you are on a fixed term, your end date is clear, and we will discuss renewal well in advance. We aim to convert fixed-term staff to permanent roles where business needs allow, but this is not guaranteed. Check your offer letter to confirm your status.

### Personal Details

It is important that our records are accurate for payroll, insurance, and emergency contacts. If your name changes (e.g., through marriage), your address, your bank account details, your emergency contact, or your next of kin details change, you must inform People Operations.

You have **2 weeks** to report any change in personal details. Please do not wait until the last minute before a pay run. Errors in banking details can delay your salary, and errors in emergency contacts can cause serious issues in a crisis. Send these updates directly to People Operations via email or the designated HR channel. We handle this data with strict confidentiality.

### Right to Work

We are required to verify your right to work in this country. Keep a copy of your passport, visa, or right-to-work documentation with your personal files. If your visa status changes, or if your right to work expires, you must inform People Operations and your manager **immediately**. Failure to maintain the legal right to work is grounds for immediate termination of employment, regardless of probation status. We cannot employ someone who cannot legally work, and we cannot take any chances with compliance.

### Job Description and Duties

Your contract includes a job description. This is a guide to the scope of your role. However, consultancy work is dynamic. You may be asked to work on different projects, with different technologies, or in different client sectors.

We expect you to be flexible within reason. If your role changes significantly (e.g., moving from data engineering to data science), we will discuss this formally. But routine adjustments to project scope do not require a contract amendment. We are a team of generalists with specialist skills; we expect you to stretch your muscles occasionally.

### Conflicts of Interest

You are employed by Harbourlight Analytics. While we encourage learning and curiosity, you cannot work for another consultancy or take freelance data work that competes with us or uses Harbourlight client data, unless you have obtained prior written permission from your manager and People Operations.

If you have a personal interest in a company that is a client or potential client of Harbourlight, you must disclose this to People Operations and your manager before you get involved in any decisions regarding that company. This is to protect you and the firm. Transparency is key. It is not about stopping you from having outside interests, but about ensuring those interests do not compromise our objectivity or your duty to us.

Who to ask: People Operations

## 5. Pay and Benefits

We believe in fair, transparent, and timely compensation. We want you to feel financially secure so you can focus on your work. We have designed our benefits package to support your health, your home life, and your professional growth.

### Salary Payment

Your salary is paid **monthly**. Payment is made on the **25th** of the month. If the 25th falls on a weekend or a public holiday, payment will be made on the **last working day before the 25th**.

For example, if the 25th is a Saturday, you will be paid on the preceding Friday. This ensures the funds are in your account before the weekend begins.

Pay slips are available via the payroll portal. Please check your first pay slip carefully to ensure your tax code and pension contributions are correct. If you spot an error, contact Finance immediately. Do not wait for the next month; errors can compound quickly.

### Salary Bands and Reviews

We operate with salary bands for each role level. This means we have a minimum and maximum salary for a Junior Analyst, a Senior Consultant, etc. This prevents us from underpaying or overpaying people randomly and helps ensure equity across the company.

We review salary bands every **April**. During this review, we assess where our compensation stands relative to the market. If the bands are adjusted, this applies to the structure, not automatically to your individual pay. Your personal salary increase is not automatic every year. Increases are tied to your performance, your contribution, and the company’s financial health. We discuss individual salary adjustments during your reviews (see Chapter 10). If you feel your salary is out of line with your peers or the market, bring it up with People Operations and your manager with evidence. Do not guess; ask. We are happy to explain the logic behind your position in the band.

### Benefits

We provide a set of benefits designed to support your health, your development, and your home life.

#### 1. Learning Budget
You have a personal learning budget of **€1,200 per year**. This is yours to use for professional development. We believe in continuous learning, especially in the fast-moving field of data. You can spend it on:
*   Online courses (Coursera, Udemy, etc.)
*   Conferences and workshops
*   Books and technical journals
*   Certifications (e.g., AWS, Azure, SQL, Project Management)
*   Coaching or mentorship sessions

**How to use it:** You do not need to ask for permission for each small purchase, but you should discuss your learning plan with your manager during your reviews. For purchases over €300, please email your manager for quick approval. For purchases under €300, just buy it and expense it. The budget resets on January 1st. Unused funds do not roll over, so please use them. It is a resource for you to use, not a pot of gold to hoard.

#### 2. Home Office Allowance
Because many of you work from home, we want your workspace to be comfortable. New starters receive a one-off home-office allowance of **€500**.
This is for ergonomic chairs, desks, monitors, or lighting. It is a one-off grant. You do not need to produce receipts for this specific €500 allowance, but it must be spent on home office equipment. If you work entirely from the office, you can use this allowance for noise-cancelling headphones, a high-quality keyboard, or other productivity-enhancing equipment for the office.
**How to claim:** Submit a simple request to Finance with the estimated cost of the items you wish to buy. We trust you to use it wisely.

#### 3. Private Health Insurance
You are covered by our private health insurance plan from **day one**. This covers GP visits, dental, optical, and specialist referrals. We want you to have access to healthcare without bureaucratic hurdles.
**How to use it:** Download the insurance app to your phone. It contains your digital card. When you visit a doctor, present the app or your card. For specialist treatments, you usually need a referral from your GP. Keep your receipts and submit them to the insurance portal via the app. If you have a major medical event, contact the insurance provider directly.

#### 4. Pension
We believe in helping you plan for the long term. We contribute **6% of your salary** to your pension pot.
To receive this employer contribution, you must contribute at least **3% of your salary** to the pension scheme.
We use a national pension scheme provider. People Operations will provide you with the enrollment forms. Please complete these as soon as you start. The sooner you join, the sooner the compound interest starts working for you. This is a significant benefit; do not leave money on the table.

#### 5. Cycle-to-Work Scheme
We participate in the Cycle-to-Work scheme. This allows you to save tax on the purchase of a bicycle and safety equipment. You pay a fixed monthly amount out of your pre-tax salary for a period (usually 12 or 24 months). At the end of the term, you can choose to buy the bike, return it, or continue paying for it at a low rate.
**How to join:** Check the internal intranet for the specific vendor we use for the scheme. It is a great way to stay active and reduce commuting costs.

Who to ask: Finance

## 6. Leave and Time Off

We want you to take your leave. Burnout helps no one, and it harms our clients. Taking time off is not a sign of weakness; it is a sign of sustainable professionalism. We have eight types of leave to support different aspects of your life. We have designed this policy to be generous but clear.

### Summary of Leave Entitlements

| Leave Type | Entitlement | How to Request |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Annual Leave** | 27 days per year + 8 public holidays | Submit request in HR portal at least 2 weeks in advance for >3 days. |
| **Sick Leave** | 10 days per year on full pay | Notify manager by 09:00 on first day of absence. Doctor's note required after 5 consecutive days. |
| **Parental Leave** | 16 weeks on full pay (Primary Carer) | Discuss with People Operations and Manager 3 months before due date. |
| **Partner Leave** | 6 weeks on full pay | Must be taken within first 6 months of child’s birth/adoption. |
| **Volunteering Leave** | 2 days per year on full pay | Submit request in HR portal like annual leave; proof of charity registration required. |
| **Bereavement Leave** | 3 days (or 5 days for partner, child, or parent) | Notify manager immediately. No need to provide documentation initially. |
| **Jury/Public Duty** | Paid at full salary for duration of duty | Provide jury summons or official document to People Operations. |
| **Unpaid Leave** | Up to 20 days per year | Agree in writing with your manager. |

### Annual Leave

You are entitled to **27 days** of annual leave per year. In addition, you have **8 public holidays** which are fixed dates set by the government and listed on our company calendar.

You can carry over unused annual leave, but with limits. You can carry over a maximum of **5 unused days** into the next calendar year. These carried-over days **must be used by 31 March** of the following year. If you do not use them by that date, they are forfeited. We encourage you to take this leave before the end of the year if possible. We do this to prevent a massive backlog of leave that could disrupt projects early in the new year.

**How to request:**
1.  Log into the HR portal.
2.  Select the dates you wish to take.
3.  Check your team calendar to ensure you are not clashing with key deliverables or other team members.
4.  Submit the request.
5.  **Notice Period:** For leave longer than **3 consecutive days**, you must give at least **2 weeks' notice**. This gives the team time to prepare.

*Note: Public holidays are not deducted from your annual leave allowance. They are separate.*

### Sick Leave

If you are too ill to work, you are entitled to **10 days per year** on **full pay**. This is for short-term illness. If you are genuinely sick, please stay home. Do not try to "push through." You will only make it worse and risk infecting colleagues.

**Procedure:**
1.  Notify your manager and your team channel by **09:00** on the first day of absence.
2.  Set your chat status to "Sick - Out of Office".
3.  Do not log in unless absolutely necessary and requested by your manager (which should be rare).

If your absence lasts for more than **5 consecutive days**, you are required to provide a **doctor's note** (medical certificate) to People Operations.

If you are ill for longer than 10 days, we will discuss your options, which may include long-term sick leave provisions under local law or unpaid leave. We will support you through the process.

### Parental Leave

We support new parents generously. We believe that bringing a new life into the world is a major event and should be treated as such.

**Primary Carer:** You are entitled to **16 weeks** of leave on **full pay**. This applies to mothers, adoptive parents, or surrogates who are the primary caregiver. This period is designed to allow for recovery and bonding.

**Partner:** Your partner is entitled to **6 weeks** of leave on **full pay**. This leave must be taken within the **first 6 months** of the child’s birth or adoption. It can be taken as one continuous block or split into separate periods, subject to agreement with your manager.

**How to request:**
1.  Once you know you are expecting or adopting, inform People Operations and your manager.
2.  We will create a transition plan for your work. This is a collaborative process, not a top-down order.
3.  Confirm your intended start and end dates at least 4 weeks before your leave begins. This allows us to secure cover and manage client expectations.

### Volunteering Leave

We encourage you to give back to your community. You are entitled to **2 days per year** of paid volunteering leave.

This leave is specifically for volunteering with a **registered charity**. You must provide proof of the charity's registration or a confirmation letter from the charity stating the dates you will be volunteering. This is not for general leisure activities or informal help; it must be organized volunteering.

**How to request:** Request this leave in the HR portal exactly as you would request annual leave. Attach the confirmation from the charity. You do not need to provide medical notes or other justification.

### Bereavement Leave

Grief is a significant life event. We offer compassionate leave.

*   **3 days** of paid leave for the death of any close relative (sibling, grandparent, aunt/uncle, etc.).
*   **5 days** of paid leave for the death of a **partner, child, or parent**.

You do not need to provide a death certificate for the initial request, but we may ask for documentation if the leave extends or if there are questions. Notify your manager as soon as possible. We will handle the workload adjustments.

### Jury and Public Duty

If you are called for jury service or other official public duty, you will be paid your **full salary** for as long as the duty lasts. You do not need to use annual leave. Civic duty is important, and we want to support your participation.

**How to request:**
1.  As soon as you receive the summons, forward a copy to People Operations.
2.  Inform your manager so they can adjust your workload.
3.  If the duty is interrupted or rescheduled, let us know.

### Unpaid Leave

If you need time off for reasons not covered by the above categories (e.g., a sabbatical, travel, caring for an elderly relative without parental provisions), you can request unpaid leave.

You can request up to **20 days per year**.
This is **not automatic**. It is **by agreement** with your manager.
You must discuss this with your manager. There is no fixed notice period mandated for unpaid leave, butwe recommend bringing it up as early as possible to allow for planning. During unpaid leave, you do not accrue annual leave, and you must consider your own pension contributions and insurance coverage. We will support you in understanding the financial implications.

Who to ask: People Operations

## 7. Health, Safety and Wellbeing

We take your safety seriously, whether you are in the office or at home. We also care about your mental health. A burnt-out team is not a productive team. We want you to thrive, not just survive.

### Office Safety

Our office is maintained to high safety standards. We do regular checks, but your eyes are the most important safety tool.
*   **First Aid:** A trained first-aider is named on the **office noticeboard**. Learn who this is. Do not wait for an emergency to look at the sign. Know where the first aid kit is stored as well.
*   **Emergency Exits:** Familiarize yourself with the fire exits and assembly point when you first visit the office. We do a fire drill once a year. Take it seriously.
*   **Hazard Reporting:** If you see a trip hazard, a broken chair, or a leaking pipe, report it immediately to the Office Manager. Do not just walk past it. If you see something that looks unsafe, say so. We would rather you flag a non-issue than miss a real one.

### Working from Home

Home offices are your responsibility, but we support you in making them safe.
*   **Workstation Self-Assessment:** Every home worker must complete a **short workstation self-assessment** in their **first month**. This is a simple checklist: Is your screen at eye level? Is your chair adjustable? Are your feet flat on the floor? Do you take breaks?
    People Operations will send you the link to this assessment. Complete it honestly. If you identify risks, talk to your manager. We may provide extra equipment or adjust your hours to help.
*   **Ergonomics:** Avoid slouching. Stand up every hour. Stretch. Eye strain is common with data work; use the 20-20-20 rule (every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds).

### Employee Assistance Line (EAP)

We provide a **confidential employee assistance line**. This is a free, external service available to all employees and their immediate family members.
*   **Usage:** You can call at any time.
*   **Topics:** Mental health, financial advice, legal advice, family issues, stress management.
*   **Confidentiality:** Harbourlight Analytics does **not** know who uses this line. We do not receive reports on individual usage. It is completely anonymous.
*   **Access:** The phone number is on your welcome pack and the intranet. Save it in your phone now, so you have it if you ever need it. Using this service is a sign of strength, not weakness.

### Stress and Burnout Prevention

We monitor workload. If you are consistently working outside core hours, or if you feel overwhelmed, speak up.
*   Your manager is responsible for monitoring team workload.
*   If you feel your workload is unsustainable, book a meeting with your manager. Say, "I am struggling to balance X and Y. I need help prioritizing or additional resources."
*   Taking breaks is mandatory. You must take a proper lunch break away from your screen. Disconnecting allows you to return with fresh eyes.

Who to ask: People Operations

## 8. Equipment, Security and Data

Data is our product. Protecting it is everyone’s job. One slip-up can lose us a client or result in legal penalties. Treat data with the same care you would treat your own bank account. We are a consultancy; our clients trust us with their most sensitive information. We must honor that trust.

### Company Equipment

All employees are provided with a company laptop.
*   **Ownership:** The laptop belongs to Harbourlight Analytics. You are responsible for its safekeeping.
*   **Encryption:** Your laptop must have **full-disk encryption** enabled. This is done automatically by IT upon setup. Do not disable it.
*   **Screen Lock:** Your laptop is configured to **automatically lock the screen after 5 minutes** of inactivity. If you leave your desk, even for a moment, lock your screen (Cmd+L on Mac, Win+L on Windows). This is a simple habit that protects against shoulder-surfing and accidental exposure.

### Data Security Rules

**Rule 1: Client Data stays on Company Systems.**
Never copy client data to your personal devices. No personal phones, no personal laptops, no personal USB drives, no personal cloud storage (like your personal Dropbox or Google Drive).
*   If you need to move data, use the company-approved secure transfer tools (e.g., SFTP, company SharePoint).
*   If you are unsure if a storage location is approved, ask IT.

**Rule 2: Password Management.**
**Password manager use is mandatory.** We provide a license for a password manager (e.g., 1Password or LastPass).
*   Do not reuse passwords.
*   Do not write passwords on sticky notes.
*   Generate strong, complex passwords using the manager.

**Rule 3: Clean Desk Policy.**
When working in the office, lock your laptop when you leave your desk. Do not leave printed client documents on your desk. Shred them when you are done. Information leaks often happen not through hacking, but through carelessness.

### Lost or Stolen Equipment

If your laptop or phone is lost or stolen, you must act immediately. Speed is essential to prevent data theft.
*   **Report to IT within 1 hour.**
*   Send an email to IT and your manager with the subject: "URGENT: Lost/Stolen Equipment - [Your Name]".
*   IT will remotely wipe the device if it is connected to the internet.
*   File a police report if you believe it was stolen.

### Software and Licensing

Only install software that is approved by IT. Do not download "free" versions of professional tools from unofficial sites. This can introduce malware or violate copyright laws. If you need a tool for work, submit a ticket to IT. They will procure the license securely. Unapproved software is a security risk and a legal liability for the company.

### Phishing and Scams

Be vigilant. We use MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) for all accounts. If you get an email asking for your password or asking you to click a link to "verify your account," it is likely a scam.
*   Do not click links in unexpected emails.
*   Check the sender’s email address carefully. Look for subtle typos or mismatched domains.
*   If in doubt, forward the email to IT for inspection. There is no penalty for reporting a false alarm; there is a high penalty for clicking a malicious link.

Who to ask: IT

## 9. Code of Conduct

This chapter outlines how we behave. It is based on our values and professional standards. As consultants, we are the face of Harbourlight to our clients. Our conduct must be beyond reproach, not just to avoid trouble, but to maintain the integrity of our work and the trust of our partners.

1.  **Honesty:** We do not lie, mislead, or omit material facts. We report time accurately and expenses truthfully. If you make a mistake, you admit it. If you don’t know an answer, you say so.
2.  **Integrity:** We act ethically even when no one is watching. We do not manipulate data to fit a desired outcome. We do not hide unfavorable results. We do not cut corners on security or compliance.
3.  **Respect:** We treat colleagues, clients, and vendors with dignity. We do not tolerate bullying, harassment, or discrimination. We listen actively. We value diverse perspectives.
4.  **Competence:** We only take on work we are qualified to do. If we are unsure, we ask for help or training. We do not overpromise on deliverables or timelines. We acknowledge our limits.
5.  **Confidentiality:** We protect client and company information strictly. We do not discuss client projects in public places like elevators, cafes, or public transport. We do not share proprietary methodologies or client data with unauthorized parties.
6.  **Fairness:** We give credit where it is due. We do not steal ideas or take credit for others’ work. We evaluate opportunities and feedback based on merit, not personal preference.
7.  **Accountability:** We admit mistakes quickly and fix them. We do not blame others for our errors. We take responsibility for the impact of our actions, even if unintended.
8.  **Professionalism:** We maintain a professional demeanor in all communications, whether written or verbal. We are punctual for meetings. We are prepared. We are polite, even when frustrated.

### Raising a Concern

If you see something wrong—if you see unethical behavior, safety hazards, fraud, or harassment—you have a duty to speak up. It is uncomfortable, but it is necessary.

*   If it is safe and appropriate, talk to the person directly. Sometimes things are misunderstandings.
*   If you are uncomfortable talking to the person, or if the issue continues, report it to your **manager**.
*   If your manager is involved in the issue, or if you are not comfortable with them, report it to **People Operations** or a senior leader.
*   You can also report concerns **anonymously** via our whistleblower portal (link on intranet).

**Protection:** **Nobody will be penalised for raising a concern in good faith.** We strictly prohibit retaliation. If you feel you are being retaliated against for raising a concern, report this immediately to the CEO or external legal counsel. We take retaliation seriously because it silences the very voices we need to keep us honest.

Who to ask: People Operations

## 10. Growth, Feedback and Reviews

We want you to grow. We invest in your career. We believe that people do their best work when they know how they are doing and where they are going. Our feedback model is continuous, not just an annual event.

### One-to-Ones

You will have a **monthly one-to-one** with your manager. This is your time. It is not just a status update. Use it to discuss career goals, challenges, and feedback. Come prepared with topics. Your manager’s role is to support you, remove blockers, and help you navigate your career.

### Formal Reviews

We conduct formal performance reviews **twice a year**, in **April** and **October**.

These are structured conversations about:
*   Your achievements against goals.
*   How you have demonstrated our values.
*   Areas for development.
*   Future goals for the next six months.

Promotions are discussed during the **April** review. If you are ready for the next level, show your evidence throughout the year. Do not wait for the review to bring up your desire for promotion. Discuss it in your one-to-ones and with your manager as you prepare.

### Feedback Culture

Feedback should be continuous.
*   **Give feedback kindly:** Be specific, timely, and constructive. Do not save up grievances for six months. Address issues as they arise.
*   **Receive feedback openly:** Listen without defending. Ask for examples. Say "thank you" and consider the input. Even if you disagree, thank the person for their perspective.

Who to ask: Your manager

## 11. Leaving Harbourlight

When you leave Harbourlight, whether you choose to or we choose to, we want to part ways with respect and professionalism. We will remember how you leave, and you will remember how we treated you.

### Resignation

Submit your resignation in writing to People Operations and your manager. Serve your notice period (4 weeks, or 1 week during probation).

### Handover

Work with your manager to complete a proper handover. Document your projects, share files, and brief your colleagues. A good handover leaves a positive last impression. It ensures your team can continue your work smoothly.

### Equipment

**Return equipment on your last day.** This includes your laptop, phone, keys, and access cards. IT will inspect them. Ensure your personal files are removed before returning the device.

### Exit Conversation

You will have an **exit conversation** with People Operations. This is a chance to give honest feedback about your time here. We use this to improve our processes. Your responses are kept confidential from your manager.

### Final Pay

**Unused annual leave is paid out** in your final paycheck. Your final salary and any pension/insurance details will be processed by Finance.

### References

After you leave, we will provide a neutral reference confirming your **dates of employment** and **job title**. We do not provide subjective performance references unless agreed in writing.

Who to ask: People Operations
