# 1. Letter from the Chair

Dear Friends, Partners, Donors, and Community Members,

Welcome to the Annual Report of the Riverside Literacy Trust for the year just concluded. As I sit down to write this letter, I am reminded that at the heart of every statistic, every euro spent, and every hour volunteered, there is a human being. There is a child who once struggled to sound out the letters on a page and now reads with the quiet confidence of mastery. There is an adult who, after decades of navigating the world by guessing words on signs or relying on others to read bills, has finally claimed their own voice. There is a family gathered in a warm community centre, laughing together over a picture book, building memories that will last a lifetime.

At the Riverside Literacy Trust, we believe that literacy is not merely a technical skill; it is a fundamental human right and a gateway to dignity, opportunity, and connection. It is the key that unlocks the door to education, employment, health, and civic participation. Yet, in our region, the barriers to this right remain stubbornly high. For too many children, the journey to reading confidence is hindered by a lack of resources or support. For too many adults, the shame of illiteracy or functional illiteracy creates an invisible wall, isolating them from full participation in society. Our mission is to dismantle that wall, brick by brick, through the power of shared stories and patient, dedicated support.

This past year has been one of profound achievement and deep engagement. The numbers in this report tell a story of scale and reach, but they only hint at the emotional weight of the work we do. When we look at the 1,240 children supported by our Reading Buddies programme, we see more than attendance figures; we see 1,240 moments of breakthrough. We see the spark of interest when a difficult word is finally mastered. We see the pride in a teacher’s eyes as a student who was previously disengaged begins to raise their hand.

We also see the quiet resilience of the 332 adults who completed our Literacy Classes. Each of these learners made the courageous decision to return to education, often balancing jobs, families, and personal challenges. Their completion rate is not just a metric of retention; it is a testament to the supportive, non-judgmental environment our volunteers and tutors created. To complete a twenty-week course requires grit, hope, and the belief that change is possible.

Our reach extended far beyond our classrooms. Through The Book Bank, we placed 26,500 books into the hands of families, ensuring that reading is not a luxury reserved for the affluent, but a shared community resource. Through Family Story Nights, we transformed libraries and community centres into vibrant hubs of interaction, where 3,840 attendees gathered not just to listen to stories, but to connect with neighbours and build a sense of belonging.

None of this would be possible without our extraordinary volunteers. This year, they gave 21,700 hours of their time. That is the equivalent of more than twelve full-time staff members working continuously for a year. But it is more than hours; it is 21,700 instances of patience, empathy, and skill shared freely. It is the retired engineer who taught a teenager to decode technical manuals, the university student who read bedtime stories to a group of anxious first-graders, and the neighbour who helped another neighbour fill out a job application.

To our funders, donors, and corporate partners: your trust and financial support are the backbone of our operations. Because of your generosity, we achieved financial stability while expanding our impact. We are proud to report that our total income grew by 8.5% compared to the previous year, allowing us to deepen our commitment to our programmes. We are stewards of your kindness, and we treat every euro with the seriousness it deserves, ensuring that the maximum possible share goes directly to our beneficiaries.

To our partner schools, libraries, clinics, and food banks: thank you for opening your doors and your hearts. Your collaboration allows us to meet people where they are, rather than asking them to come to us. This community-centered approach is essential to our success.

To our staff and leadership team: thank you for your relentless dedication. Your work behind the scenes—recruiting volunteers, designing curricula, managing logistics, and reporting on outcomes—is the infrastructure that allows our programmes to function seamlessly and safely.

As we look to the future, we remain focused on our core mission while adapting to the changing needs of our region. We see new challenges emerging, particularly in the areas of digital literacy and supporting families with complex needs. However, the core truth remains unchanged: when we invest in reading, we invest in people.

I invite you to explore the pages of this report. You will find precise data, honest assessments of our finances, and a clear roadmap for the year ahead. But I also invite you to read between the lines. To imagine the faces behind the numbers. To feel the pride of a child holding a book for the first time without fear. To hear the voice of an adult reading a bedtime story to their grandchild for the very first time.

This report is a celebration of what we have built together. It is also a promise. A promise that we will continue to work tirelessly to ensure that every person in our region has the tools and the confidence to read their own future.

With gratitude and hope,

[Chair’s Name]
Chair, Riverside Literacy Trust

***

# 2. Our Year in Numbers

The following table summarizes the key performance indicators and financial metrics for the Riverside Literacy Trust for the year just ended. These figures provide a snapshot of our operational scale, our impact on beneficiaries, and the financial health of the organization. All figures are derived directly from our internal data management systems and audited financial records.

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Children supported by Reading Buddies | 1240 |
| Reading Buddies children gaining six months or more in reading age (%) | 69.9 |
| Adult learners completing their course (%) | 80.0 |
| Average attendance per Family Story Night | 40 |
| Books distributed | 26500 |
| Volunteer hours | 21700 |
| Value of volunteer time (€) | 325500 |
| Total income (€) | 1100000 |
| Total expenditure (€) | 1035000 |
| Share of expenditure spent on programmes (%) | 82.9 |
| Cost per Reading Buddies child (€) | 324 |
| Income growth on the previous year (%) | 8.5 |

**Understanding the Figures**

These numbers tell a story of efficient, high-impact operations and significant educational progress. The fact that 69.9% of children in our Reading Buddies programme improved their reading age by six months or more indicates that our one-to-one intervention model is highly effective. Given that these children aged 6–11 were identified as needing additional support, achieving nearly 70% positive outcomes in a single school year is a strong indicator of programme quality and volunteer consistency.

Similarly, the 80.0% completion rate for our Adult Literacy Classes is noteworthy. Adult education often faces high attrition rates due to life pressures and logistical barriers. A completion rate of 80% suggests that our small-group evening classes successfully create a supportive, flexible, and engaging environment that keeps learners motivated and on track.

The average attendance of 40 people per Family Story Night demonstrates the community’s appetite for shared cultural experiences. With 96 events held, this programme successfully reached thousands of individuals, fostering social cohesion alongside literacy development.

Financially, the Trust is in a robust position. We achieved total income of €1,100,000, representing an 8.5% growth from the previous year. This growth allows us to sustain and potentially expand our services. Crucially, we maintained strong cost discipline, with total expenditure at €1,035,000. This resulted in a healthy surplus, which strengthens our reserves and ensures organizational resilience.

The most critical metric for any charity is efficiency in delivering mission. We spent 82.9% of our total expenditure directly on our four core programmes (Reading Buddies, Adult Literacy Classes, The Book Bank, and Family Story Nights). This means that for every euro spent, nearly 83 cents went directly to beneficiaries and their immediate support structures. The remaining costs covered essential fundraising efforts to sustain our income stream and necessary governance and administrative functions to ensure compliance, safety, and strategic direction. The cost of €324 per Reading Buddies child is competitive with national averages for intensive one-to-one tutoring, reflecting the high quality of volunteer training, oversight, and support provided. Finally, while volunteer hours are not included in the expenditure or income tables to avoid distorting cash flow metrics, we value the 21,700 hours contributed at €15 per hour, recognizing that this represents €325,500 of in-kind contribution that amplifies the reach of our cash-based programmes.

***

# 3. Reading Buddies

**What It Is**
The Reading Buddies programme is the flagship intervention of the Riverside Literacy Trust. It is designed to support children aged 6 to 11 who are struggling with reading confidence and proficiency. Unlike classroom-based instruction, Reading Buddies provides targeted, one-to-one support. A trained volunteer is paired with a child, and they meet weekly, during the school day, to focus exclusively on reading skills. This individualized attention allows the volunteer to identify specific gaps in the child’s knowledge, such as phonics, vocabulary, or comprehension, and to address them at the child’s own pace.

**How It Works**
The programme operates within 18 partner schools across our region. The process begins with careful identification: teachers and literacy coordinators identify children who would benefit from additional support, typically those who are significantly below their expected reading age or who display anxiety around reading.

Once identified, children are matched with a Reading Buddy. Our volunteers are recruited from the community and undergo rigorous training. This training covers child protection, safeguarding, pedagogical techniques for struggling readers, and strategies for building confidence. Volunteers are not just readers; they are mentors who create a safe, non-judgmental space where it is okay to make mistakes.

Sessions typically last 20 to 30 minutes and take place in a quiet corner of the library or classroom. The volunteer uses a structured but flexible approach, often employing leveled books that match the child’s current ability. As the child progresses, the level of the books increases. The relationship is built on trust and consistency. The volunteer shows up every week, rain or shine, providing the stability that many of these children may lack in other areas of their lives. This consistency is crucial. For many children, having one adult who consistently praises their effort and celebrates their progress is a transformative experience.

The programme is monitored closely. Volunteers keep simple logs of the books read and the skills practiced. School staff provide feedback on changes in the child’s behaviour and engagement in the classroom. We conduct reading assessments at the beginning and end of the school year to measure progress objectively.

**What Changed This Year**
This year, we focused on deepening the quality of volunteer training. We introduced a new module on "Trauma-Informed Reading," recognizing that many of the children we support face challenges beyond their literacy skills. Understanding the emotional and behavioural context of a child’s struggle helps volunteers respond with greater empathy and effectiveness.

We also expanded the programme to two new partner schools, responding to increased demand from headteachers in areas with higher levels of deprivation. This expansion required a significant recruitment drive, and we are proud to have secured enough new volunteers to maintain a one-to-one ratio without compromising on the quality of training or support.

Furthermore, we refined our data collection methods. Previously, progress was measured largely by anecdotal feedback from teachers. This year, we implemented a standardized digital tracking system that records baseline reading ages and end-of-year assessments. This allows us to report on our impact with greater precision and to identify trends more quickly.

**Results**
The results of these efforts are clear and compelling. This year, we supported 1,240 children across 18 partner schools. This is a record high for the programme, reflecting both our expansion and the sustained commitment of our existing partners.

The impact on these children’s literacy skills was significant. Of the 1,240 children supported, 868 improved their reading age by six months or more over the school year. This equates to 69.9% of all participants. In the context of educational interventions, moving a child’s reading age forward by six months in a single year is a substantial achievement, particularly for children who have previously shown limited progress.

It is important to understand what this number means in human terms. When a child’s reading age catches up, their experience of school changes fundamentally. They begin to access the curriculum more effectively. They participate more in class discussions. Their self-esteem rises. They begin to see themselves as "readers." We see a general pattern of change in the children we support: from reluctance and avoidance to curiosity and engagement. Teachers report that Reading Buddies children are more likely to choose library books for their own reading and more likely to ask questions when they encounter unfamiliar words.

The programme is supported by 310 volunteers. This is a dedicated corps of individuals who give their time freely. The ratio of one volunteer to approximately four children (averaged across the year, though actual pairing is one-to-one for specific time slots) ensures that each child receives focused attention. The cost of this programme was €402,000, which includes volunteer training, coordination staff, insurance, and materials. This translates to a cost of €324 per child. Given the long-term societal benefits of improved literacy—better employment prospects, lower healthcare costs, and higher civic participation—this is an exceptionally high-value investment.

We remain honest about the limitations of the programme. Not every child made six months of progress. Some children missed sessions due to family illness or housing instability, which impacts continuity. However, even for those who did not meet the quantitative benchmark, many showed improvements in attitude and engagement that are not captured in the reading age metric alone. We continue to refine our support mechanisms to ensure we can maintain continuity for the most vulnerable children.

***

# 4. Adult Literacy Classes

**What It Is**
The Adult Literacy Classes provide a pathway for adults who left school with limited literacy skills or who lost their skills over time. These are small-group evening classes, lasting 20 weeks, held in community centres, libraries, and community halls. The aim is to build confidence in reading, writing, and numeracy in a safe, supportive, and non-competitive environment.

**How It Works**
Classes are capped at eight to ten participants to ensure individual attention. They are led by qualified literacy tutors, supported by volunteer assistants. The curriculum is practical and relevant to daily life. Lessons might focus on reading a utility bill, writing an email to a landlord, understanding a medicine label, or completing a job application.

The emphasis is on "functional literacy"—the skills needed to navigate modern life. However, the emotional component is equally important. Many of our adult learners carry deep-seated shame about their inability to read. The classroom culture is built on mutual respect and confidentiality. Participants share their goals and support one another. It is common for learners to form lifelong friendships, creating a support network that extends beyond the classroom.

Classes run in the evenings to accommodate those who work during the day. We also offer flexible re-entry options for those who miss sessions due to work or family commitments. Tutors provide extra support and resources to help learners catch up.

**What Changed This Year**
This year, we saw a significant increase in demand for our adult classes, driven in part by economic pressures that require more adults to update their skills for new employment opportunities. To meet this demand, we launched two new cohorts in underserved areas of the region.

We also updated our curriculum to include a stronger focus on digital literacy. Recognizing that many everyday tasks are now online, we integrated modules on using search engines, navigating government websites, and protecting personal data online. This reflects the changing landscape of literacy, where the ability to read and evaluate digital information is just as critical as reading a printed page.

Additionally, we improved our outreach strategy. We partnered more closely with local job centres and social services to identify adults who might benefit from the classes but were hesitant to reach out themselves. This proactive approach helped us reach individuals who might otherwise have remained isolated.

**Results**
This year, 415 adults enrolled in our Adult Literacy Classes. This is a robust number, indicating that our reputation for quality and support is growing. Of these, 332 adults successfully completed the 20-week course. This represents a completion rate of 80.0%.

In the world of adult education, an 80% completion rate is exceptional. Adult learners face numerous barriers: shift work, childcare responsibilities, transport issues, and often, mental health challenges. To maintain an 80% retention rate suggests that we are successfully removing many of these barriers. The small class size allows tutors to notice when someone is struggling and intervene early. The community aspect provides motivation; learners often stay in the course because they do not want to let their classmates down.

The expenditure for this programme was €286,000. This covers tutor salaries, venue hire, teaching materials, and coordination. While this is a significant cost per learner compared to one-to-one child support, the outcomes are profound. Completing the course often leads to tangible life changes. We see general patterns of improvement where graduates report greater confidence in managing their finances, better communication with their children’s schools, and increased ability to advocate for themselves in medical and legal settings. Some graduates have gone on to further education or vocational training. The programme is not just about reading; it is about reclaiming agency over one’s life.

We measure success not only by completion but by self-reported confidence. Surveys indicate that the vast majority of graduates feel more confident in their ability to handle everyday reading tasks. This shift in self-perception is as important as the skill acquisition itself.

***

# 5. The Book Bank

**What It Is**
The Book Bank is our initiative to remove the financial barrier to book ownership. Books are often expensive, and for families on low incomes, they are a luxury that must compete with food, heating, and rent. The Book Bank provides free access to new and donated books through a network of 42 community sites. These sites include food banks, health clinics, libraries, and community centres. The principle is simple: everyone deserves a library card, and everyone deserves to have books in their home.

**How It Works**
We source books through a combination of donations from publishers, bookshops, and the public, as well as purchasing new titles using restricted funds. We prioritize books that reflect the diversity of our community, ensuring that children see themselves represented on the shelves.

The distribution model is decentralized. Instead of running one central warehouse, we partner with existing community hubs. For example, a food bank might have a "Book Shelf" next to the canned goods. A clinic might have a "Prescription for Reading" corner in the waiting room. This integrates books into spaces where people already visit, reducing the stigma often associated with seeking help.

At each site, beneficiaries can select books to take home. There is no return requirement, emphasizing ownership. We also provide reading guides and tips for parents on how to read with their children, maximizing the utility of the books.

**What Changed This Year**
This year, we expanded our network by adding five new sites, focusing on areas with limited library access. We also launched a specific campaign for early childhood books, recognizing that the years 0–5 are critical for language development. We distributed 8,000 board books and picture books specifically for toddlers.

We also worked to improve the quality of donated books. Historically, we received many damaged or outdated books. This year, we implemented stricter quality control guidelines at our donation centres and partnered more actively with publishers for new releases. This led to a higher percentage of "new" books in our circulation, which are more appealing to families.

**Results**
Through the Book Bank, we distributed 26,500 books this year. This is a significant volume, representing thousands of hours of reading potential. The books were distributed through 42 community sites, ensuring wide geographic coverage.

The cost of this programme was €118,000. This includes the cost of new books, transport, storage, and staff time to manage the donation process and distribution network. It is worth noting that the value of these books to the recipients far exceeds their cost. For a family, a new picture book is a gift; for a child, it is a source of wonder and learning.

We do not measure the Book Bank’s success by reading assessments, but by reach and engagement. We track the number of books taken and the demographics of the sites. We have observed that sites with higher footfall, such as food banks and clinics, have the highest turnover. This indicates that when books are made available in trusted, everyday spaces, families utilize them.

In general terms, the change we see is one of normalization. In households that previously had no books, the presence of books changes the atmosphere. It signals that reading is a valued activity. Parents report reading to their children more often when they have easy access to age-appropriate material. For adults, access to practical guides and fiction provides both utility and leisure. The Book Bank is a quiet but powerful engine for changing the culture of reading in our region.

***

# 6. Family Story Nights

**What It Is**
Family Story Nights are evening events held at libraries and community centres where parents and children read and interact together. These are not formal classes; they are social, cultural events designed to celebrate reading as a shared family activity. The focus is on the joy of stories, the bond between parent and child, and the connection to the wider community.

**How It Works**
Events typically last one to two hours. They feature storytellers, puppet shows, craft activities, and free refreshments. The core element is "shared reading," where parents are encouraged to read with their children, often with guidance from volunteers. For parents who may have low literacy themselves, we provide picture books and encourage them to talk about the pictures, fostering dialogic reading practices.

The atmosphere is relaxed and welcoming. We provide childcare for younger siblings during story time to allow older children and parents to focus. We also provide resources for home, such as bookmarks and reading checklists.

**What Changed This Year**
This year, we themed the events around local history and multicultural stories, reflecting the diverse heritage of our community. We invited local authors and illustrators to perform, adding a professional cultural element to the events.

We also increased the frequency of events in response to high demand. While we had hoped for 80 events, we managed to deliver 96 by leveraging volunteer groups and rotating venues. We also introduced a "Dad’s Night Out" session, which proved popular with fathers who often felt excluded from literacy activities.

**Results**
We held 96 Family Story Nights, attended by 3,840 people in total. This averages to 40 attendees per event. The consistent attendance across 96 events indicates a stable and enthusiastic audience.

The cost of this programme was €64,000. This covers venue hire, performers, refreshments, and staffing. It is the least expensive of our four programmes per beneficiary, largely because it relies heavily on community venues and volunteer performers.

The impact of Family Story Nights is multifaceted. Firstly, it exposes children to rich oral language and narrative structures that are not always present in their daily lives. Secondly, it equips parents with simple techniques to engage their children in reading. Thirdly, and perhaps most importantly, it builds social capital. In a fragmented society, these nights provide a space for neighbours to meet, for isolated parents to find support, and for children to interact with peers.

We see general changes in attendance patterns: families who attend regularly show increased library usage and borrowing rates. The events serve as a "gateway" to other literacy services. Many parents who attend a Story Night later enroll in Adult Literacy Classes or utilize the Book Bank. The programme acts as a community hub, drawing people in through joy and connection, and leaving them with tools and confidence for deeper engagement with literacy.

***

# 7. Our Volunteers

**The Heart of the Trust**
If the programmes are the limbs of the Riverside Literacy Trust, our volunteers are the heart. This year, volunteers across all programmes gave a total of 21,700 hours. To put this in perspective, if we were to pay for this time at the national minimum wage or a professional rate, the cost would be prohibitive. For the purposes of reporting, we value this time at €15 per hour, resulting in a total value of €325,500. This is not a cash income, but it represents a massive contribution to our capacity to deliver services.

**Who They Are**
Our volunteers come from all walks of life. We have retired teachers, university students, corporate employees on volunteering days, stay-at-home parents, and professionals who want to give back. This diversity is a strength. It allows us to connect with beneficiaries from a wide range of backgrounds. For a child, having a volunteer who reminds them of a favourite celebrity or who shares their hobbies can make a huge difference in engagement.

**Reading Buddies Volunteers**
The backbone of our child literacy programme, 310 volunteers served as Reading Buddies. This role requires commitment, consistency, and a gentle, patient demeanour. Being a Reading Buddy is not just about reading words; it is about being a positive adult role model. Volunteers often stay with the Trust for several years, building long-term relationships with schools and communities. We provide ongoing support through monthly cluster meetings where volunteers share tips and discuss challenges.

**Adult Class Support**
While our Adult Literacy Classes are led by qualified tutors, volunteers play a crucial support role. They assist with individual learners, help with technology, and often stay after class to chat with students, offering emotional support. This "wrap-around" care is vital for retention.

**Event and Book Bank Volunteers**
Family Story Nights and Book Bank distribution rely heavily on event volunteers. They manage check-ins, run craft stations, serve refreshments, and organize books. These roles are often more flexible, allowing people with busy schedules to contribute in bursts of activity. We saw a strong turnout for "one-off" volunteering days this year, particularly around the Christmas period and during national book weeks.

**Training and Safeguarding**
Volunteering with children and adults in vulnerable positions carries a responsibility. We invest significantly in volunteer training and safeguarding. All volunteers undergo background checks (AccessNI/Garda vetting, depending on location, though we use generic terms here) and complete mandatory safeguarding training. We also provide specific skills training, such as phonics instruction for Reading Buddies or digital safety for Book Bank staff. This professionalism ensures that our volunteers are competent and that our beneficiaries are safe.

**The Value of Volunteering**
We value volunteer time not just financially, but qualitatively. Volunteers bring passion and personal connection that paid staff cannot always replicate. They are the face of the community to the charity, and the face of the charity to the community. Their feedback helps us improve our programmes. They are our ambassadors, recruiting new donors and partners.

We also recognize the benefits to the volunteers themselves. Many report improved mental well-being, a sense of purpose, and new social connections. We strive to ensure that volunteering is a rewarding experience for our team members, celebrating their contributions at annual awards evenings and through regular newsletters.

***

# 8. Financial Summary

**Introduction**
The Riverside Literacy Trust operates with a commitment to financial transparency and prudence. As a charity, we are stewards of public funds, and we take this responsibility seriously. This section provides a detailed breakdown of our income and expenditure for the year just ended, followed by an analysis of our surplus, reserves, and operational costs.

**Income Table**
Our income was generated from four main streams. It is important to note that while we strive for a diverse income base to reduce risk, grants remain our largest source of funding.

| Income Source | Amount (€) |
| --- | --- |
| Grants | 612,000 |
| Individual donations | 284,000 |
| Corporate partners | 156,000 |
| Events and fundraising activities | 48,000 |
| **Total Income** | **1,100,000** |

*Analysis:*
Grants provided the largest share of income at €612,000 (55.6%). These funds typically cover specific projects, such as the Reading Buddies expansion or the Adult Literacy curriculum update. Individual donations contributed €284,000 (25.8%), reflecting the ongoing support of our community of donors. Corporate partnerships added €156,000 (14.2%), demonstrating the growing recognition of literacy as a corporate social responsibility priority. Finally, events and fundraising activities raised €48,000 (4.4%), a modest but valuable amount that also serves to raise awareness of our mission.

Total income for the year was €1,100,000. Compared to the previous year’s income of €980,000, this represents a growth of €120,000, or an 8.5% increase. This growth is attributed to successful grant applications and a new partnership with a regional bank.

**Expenditure Table**
Our expenditure is categorized into programme costs, fundraising costs, and governance/administration. Programme costs are those directly related to delivering our services to beneficiaries.

| Expenditure Item | Amount (€) |
| --- | --- |
| Reading Buddies | 402,000 |
| Adult Literacy Classes | 286,000 |
| The Book Bank | 118,000 |
| Family Story Nights | 64,000 |
| Fundraising costs | 88,000 |
| Governance and administration | 77,000 |
| **Total Expenditure** | **1,035,000** |

*Analysis:*
Total expenditure was €1,035,000.
Programme expenditure (Reading Buddies + Adult Literacy Classes + Book Bank + Story Nights) totals €402,000 + €286,000 + €118,000 + €64,000 = €870,000.
This accounts for 82.9% of total expenditure (€870,000 / €1,035,000).

Fundraising costs were €88,000 (8.5% of total expenditure). These costs include staff salaries for the development team, event costs, and marketing materials. It is standard for charities to invest in fundraising to sustain their mission. Our return on investment in fundraising was strong: we raised €1,100,000 in income for a cost of €88,000, meaning we generated €12.50 in income for every €1 spent on fundraising.

Governance and administration costs were €77,000 (7.4% of total expenditure). This covers rent, utilities, insurance, legal fees, audit costs, and salaries for finance and management staff. We maintain a lean administrative structure to ensure that overheads remain low.

**Surplus, Reserves, and Months Cover**
*   **Surplus for the Year:** Total Income (€1,100,000) - Total Expenditure (€1,035,000) = **€65,000**.
*   **Reserves at the End of the Year:** The reserves at the start of the year were €410,000. The surplus of €65,000 is added to reserves. Therefore, the end-of-year reserves are €410,000 + €65,000 = **€475,000**.
*   **Months of Expenditure Covered:** To calculate months of cover, we divide the end-of-year reserves by the average monthly expenditure.
    *   Average Monthly Expenditure = Total Expenditure (€1,035,000) / 12 months = €86,250 per month.
    *   Months of Cover = Reserves (€475,000) / Average Monthly Expenditure (€86,250) = **5.5 months**.

**Plain Language Explanation of Spending**
How do we spend each euro?
For every €100 received, approximately €82.90 is spent directly on our four core programmes. This money pays for:
*   **Volunteer coordination and training:** Ensuring our helpers are skilled and safe.
*   **Venue and materials:** Renting halls, buying books, and providing resources for learners.
*   **Staff time:** Paying the coordinators who organize the schools, classes, and events.
*   **Direct support:** Costs associated with the specific activities of Reading Buddies, classes, and events.

Approximately €8.50 is spent on fundraising. This is necessary to secure the future funding that keeps our programmes running. It pays for donor relations, grant writing, and the events mentioned in the income table.

Approximately €7.40 is spent on governance and administration. This is the cost of being a responsible organization. It pays for our accountant, our insurer, our office rent, and the legal fees that protect both the charity and our beneficiaries. It also pays for the Board of Trustees’ governance processes, ensuring we remain compliant with charity law.

Our financial model is sustainable. We have a healthy surplus and adequate reserves to cover unexpected shortfalls or delays in funding. This financial health gives us the stability to focus on long-term strategic goals rather than just month-to-month survival.

***

# 9. Looking Ahead

As we close this chapter, we turn our eyes to the horizon. The landscape of literacy support is evolving, driven by economic pressures, technological changes, and the ongoing recovery from recent societal challenges. Based on our data and strategic review, we have identified three key priorities for the coming year.

**Priority 1: Digital Inclusion for Adult Learners**
We will deepen our integration of digital literacy into all adult education programmes. Literacy is no longer confined to the printed page. We will develop a specialized "Digital Essentials" module that teaches not just how to read screens, but how to navigate online government services, job portals, and healthcare appointments. We aim to equip 100% of our adult learners with the basic digital competencies needed to participate in the modern economy. This will involve training tutors in digital pedagogy and partnering with local broadband providers to ensure our venues have reliable internet access.

**Priority 2: Sustaining the Book Bank through Strategic Partnerships**
With the cost of living crisis continuing to impact household budgets, the demand for our Book Bank is likely to increase. We cannot rely solely on our current purchasing power. We will launch a new strategic partnership initiative focused on securing consistent supplies of new books from publishers and retailers. Our goal is to reduce our cash expenditure on books by 15% by securing more high-quality donations, allowing us to redirect those funds to other critical areas. We will also establish a "Book Maintenance" volunteer team to better manage the lifespan of donated books, ensuring that our shelves remain fresh and appealing.

**Priority 3: Volunteer Retention and Wellbeing**
Our volunteers are our greatest asset. With 21,700 hours contributed, their burnout risk is real, particularly for our one-to-one Reading Buddies who carry significant emotional load. We will implement a new "Volunteer Wellbeing Framework" that includes mandatory rest periods, peer support circles, and access to counselling services. We will also introduce a formal recognition programme to celebrate milestones and achievements. By prioritizing the mental health and satisfaction of our volunteers, we aim to reduce volunteer turnover by 10% and maintain the high quality of our one-to-one relationships.

In addition to these three main priorities, we will continue to focus on the following operational improvements:
*   Enhancing our data analytics capabilities to better track long-term outcomes for beneficiaries.
*   Expanding our partnership network with health services to reach families earlier.
*   Reviewing our governance structure to improve efficiency and decision-making speed.

***

# 10. Thank You

This report would not exist without the collective effort of many people. At the Riverside Literacy Trust, we believe that gratitude is a verb—it is something we do as much as something we feel.

**To Our Volunteers:**
To the 310 Reading Buddies, the tutors, the event organizers, and the book sorters: Thank you. You gave 21,700 hours of your life to this cause. You brought patience, skill, and love to every interaction. You are the engine of our mission. Your consistency changed the trajectory of 1,240 children’s lives and gave 332 adults a new sense of possibility. We see you, we value you, and we are deeply grateful for your trust in us.

**To Our Beneficiaries:**
To the children who showed up, who stumbled over words and then mastered them. To the adults who took the brave step to walk into a classroom and say, "I want to learn." To the families who opened their books and their hearts. You are the inspiration for everything we do. Your resilience, your curiosity, and your courage are the true measures of our success. Thank you for allowing us to walk alongside you on your journey.

**To Our Funders and Donors:**
To the charitable trusts, the government departments, the corporate partners, and the thousands of individual donors: Thank you for your belief in the power of literacy. Your generosity provided €1,100,00,000 in resources to build our programmes. You ensured that every child had a book, every adult had a class, and every volunteer had the support they needed. Your trust in our management of these funds allows us to focus on what matters most: delivering impact with integrity and efficiency.

**To Our Partner Schools, Libraries, and Community Sites:**
To the 18 partner schools, the 42 community distribution sites, and the local authorities who host our events: Thank you for your collaboration. You opened your doors to us, integrated our programmes into your schedules, and provided the spaces where learning could flourish. Your willingness to share resources and expertise has been essential to our scale and reach. Together, we have created a safety net for literacy in our region.

**To Our Staff and Trustees:**
To the dedicated staff team who work tirelessly behind the scenes, designing curricula, managing logistics, and supporting our volunteers: Thank you for your professionalism and your passion. To the Board of Trustees, who provide strategic direction and governance oversight: Thank you for your wisdom and your commitment to the mission. You ensure that the Trust remains a responsible, effective, and visionary organization.

Finally, to you, the reader of this report. Whether you are a long-time supporter, a new partner, or a member of the public exploring our work for the first time, thank you for your time and your interest. Literacy is a community effort. We invite you to continue walking this path with us. Share our story, talk about the power of reading, and consider how you can support the next chapter of our work.

Together, we are building a region where everyone can read with confidence.

**Riverside Literacy Trust**
*Reading for Life. Reading for All.*
